samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Richard M. Becker was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Richard M. Becker. Mr. Becker served with the U.S. Navy. He served in the Pacific Theater, and he was on board the supply ship Antares when the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor. That was the first ship attacked on December 7th. Mr. Becker's highest rank was lieutenant JG. I'm Tom Swope, and this recording was made at Mr. Becker's home in Geneva, Ohio, on February 22nd, 2002. Dick was 80 at the time of this recording. So when did you join the service?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: 1939. And that's a crazy thing. The Navy had adopted a program where if you were under 18 and you enlisted, they only accepted you for what they called a "kiddie cruise," which is you would go in until your 21st birthday, and then you would have to reenlist or ship over or you'd go home. It was a short term. So I came right out of high school and went right down, and I was 17. And I enlisted on the kiddie cruise, except the Navy was on a quantity basis where they would take as they needed. You just couldn't walk in and join up. So I was put on hold and said to go home and we'll call you when we want you. Well, they didn't call me until after I turned 18, and then the Navy had just changed that program from four years to a six-year enlistment, so I had to go in for six years in '39. And I had nothing better to do. I had no prospect to go into school. My father couldn't afford that, for college or anything. And work effort, jobs were scarce, so it seemed a logical thing to do. At the same time that I went in, I had this strong desire to learn to fly. And of course, this gave me some moneys, which I could then devote to flying. So I started my own private flying lessons. Now when I went aboard ship, became quite a problem because the ship movement--this old bugger used to roam the whole wide Pacific all over. I developed a friendship with one of the quartermasters, who was a guy who works on the bridge to help with the navigation, charting and the sunsites and all that sort of stuff. And this quartermaster could then let me know--he had access to the ship's log. He could let me know when the ship was going to leave, when it was due back. That was rather classified information, but he would come down and share this. And that way I could schedule my time to learn to fly when I knew the ship was going to be in port because you couldn't just walk over to the airport and say, "Hey, I want to take instruction." You had to be on the schedule. So the majority of my training, flight training, this is while I was on the ship doing my other chores. And incidentally, I was pretty remote from up at the topside. I was down in the fireroom and engine room. But the odd thing was the skipper, through Esterowitz (ph), this quartermaster, some of the conversations, he knew that I was taking flying lessons, and he didn't frown on that. He looked with favor upon that. Well, of course, I was scheduled to fly the morning of the 7th at the--that is what John Rogers Airport in Honolulu was nothing but a cinder strip when I was doing this. You know, for the inner island airways there was no scheduled airline service. The only one that was flying was the China Clippers, the big old bull wings, and they were strictly water boats that landed in the harbor, and they didn't need the airport. But I was scheduled to go over that morning, and, of course, the war interrupted that. They shut everything down. And I immediately did go to the commanding officer of the ship and suggested--because I knew--one of the trips when we were off with the ship--I think we went to Midway Island to take a contingent out there and some men and equipment. On the return trip the cruiser divisions were out exercising, and one of the small airplanes, the observation airplanes, they could launch: they fire them from a catapult and then retrieve them. The guy had gotten some engine problems and landed on the water adjacent to us, and his ship was way the hell off. He was quite aways from home. So we took him aboard and put that thing on the aft, aft of the deck right there by--ahead of the boats. And my compartment was right down below so I had a chance to visit with this guy and, hell, here he is a sailor; he's a white hat. They were using those guys already. And I got into a long conversation with him, and he told me about the program and he says, "Well, there's hardly any of us get chosen, but try it. Give it a try and go at it." So when the war started and things--I had first went to the commanding officer and asked him to recommend me for blimps, lighter-than-air, and all of those classes were filled up, and he, with much regret, said, "I can't get you in there." Now I learned from this other sailor we picked up that they were flying the airplanes also, and so I went back to him. And prior to Pearl Harbor, I had asked him about it, and he said, "Yes. Put--go through the formal channels and the engineering officer to get him to approve the request and all that." But this guy sat on things and didn't want me to leave the ship and wouldn't do anything until after the war started. I went back and circumvented him, which never should do--chain of command, you know. But I did go up and request an audience with the commander officer. And he said, "Yeah." He said, "Well, you resubmit the paperwork." And he says, "I'll see that Mr. Sawny (ph) reacts and does something." And sure as hell--let me get this right now. Yeah, in April he came back and said for me to leave the ship, go to the receiving station for transportation back to the States to enroll in the program commencing on the 26th of May of '42. So I left the ship and came back. And while I was in the receiving ship--and that was a real ordeal because they used us principally in the salvage operations and working on, you know, raising the battleships and all the mess that was there. And man, I sure didn't like that at all, but somebody had to do it. In fact, we were still burying bodies as we were following the ship down the compartments down to the pumping, you know, and then on raising. I worked mostly on the battleship California and found bodies in the compartments, you know, and the crabs had already ate them up pretty good. But bring them out and give them a burial. But anyway, I did get to come back to the States and started the formal Navy training, and I graduated. Up there is my diploma. You can see that later on. It says I'm a first-class aviation pilot. That's the sailor with the white hat. He's a petty officer. In fact, I have on my other little thing down there the red markings. That's the enlisted ratings that I held. I got up to chief petty officer. And on the right is my commissioned rank because then I was commissioned. But now that's a cute thing too. I had come along as a chief petty officer. I made a fairly favorable salary as far as the enlisted rank went. In fact, I made more money than an ensign, which is the lowest--well, not the lowest, the warrant ratings. They didn't use the warrant ratings in the aviation pilot. They went from chief to promoted them directly to ensign. But even at that, I had to take a cut in pay, and I was--I had already gotten married because when I came back from my flight training, I met my wife. And I went to New Orleans to take elimination training first. That's where I met her. And by the time the commission came around, which was in '44--yeah, we were married and thinking about raising a family and all that, and that was a tough decision to take to make the pay cut. But I had been given this real desirable duty at the Naval Air Test Center. They had just commissioned a new test facility, and here I had the opportunity to fly all these airplanes. But I couldn't because the white hat sailor couldn't handle secret documents, so I wasn't permitted on the projects, and I was just being a utility pilot. Rather disgusting and discouraging because we took all the same formal training with the cadets and the Annapolis graduates. Same classrooms, same syllabus completely. But being a sailor, you're low man on the totem pole. But anyway, I talked it over with my wife, we made up our mind, and I took the commission, and then that opened all the doors, of course, and I really got to fly all sorts of things, and completed the war years. I was still in, of course, because they wouldn't--at the end of the war they instituted a program of a point system they called it. If you were overseas, if you had engaged in any battles, and how many years of service. All this sort of thing accumulated points to determine who could get out first. But this only applied to the reserves. It did not apply to the regular Navy. Now, when I took the--accepted the commission, I used to carry my enlisted file folder with me to all of the ships and stations. Somewhere that fell in the crack, and I never noticed that my enlistment expired. My six years were long gone, and I was still with the commission, and they hadn't shipped me over and, you know, upgraded the enlisted file, because the appointments that you received in the commission rank were only temporary appointments. You carried USN(T) in parentheses if you were enlisted promoted. Well, I did change my mind about making it a career after eight years and decided--my wife said, "Hey, we can't raise a family this way. You're sitting in China. I'm home here." And what the hell ever. So I decided to get out, and then became the problem--or the problem became, you know--reared its ugly head. How do you get out because they're not accepting resignations of regular Navy? And I was rooming with an old sea daddy in San Diego. I had come back to the States. That was another thing that influenced my decision to get out. I had been in the China, Japan, Okinawa, Philippine area for over a year, and the normal tour was 18 months. And I came back with a kidney stone and was hospitalized. So I was only out there about 14 months, short of the 18 months that I should have been there. And when I went for reassignment back to the West Coast--I got out of the hospital in Houston, Texas; I went back to reassignment--same little guy is sitting there, you know, with a smirk. He says, "Jeez, you never completed your last tour. We've got to send you back out." I said, "Okay. What the hell, six months or something, and I'll go back out and finish." He says, "Oh, no. You've been out for shore duty. Now you've got to go back out for another 18-month tour duty." I had only been in the hospital about a little over two months, and I was given temporary additional duty until he was going to make this assignment. So I was only back in the States about three months, and here they're going to send me out for another 18. And I said, Jesus, that can't--it's no way we can do that, handle that. The old guy I was rooming with, he was getting out of the Navy. He was like 28 years in, and he was getting out. And he was the kind of a sea duty lawyer. He just kind of knew all of the workings of the military system. And he was commissioned. And he says, "Well, hell," he says--we had long conversations. And he said, "Well, you know, nowhere have you mentioned that you shipped over," he said, "so what in the hell are you doing here if you--this is already eight years gone?" And he says, "Your enlistment was only six years." He said, "Dick, they can't hold you. They don't have any strings on you." And he says, "The way you do this is you go back to the"--Harry Truman was President at the time. And with a commission, you've got to go to the Commander-in-Chief. So I wrote my letter to the Honorable Harry Truman requesting--oh, this old guy figured it out. He says, "Don't tell them you want to go home. Just tell them you want to resign the commission and be reverted to your enlisted status. You no longer desire to hold a commission." So I did all of this, and I got this nice letter back from Harry over there. And I go back, and they suddenly discover, the personnel says, "My goodness. We have to ship you over. You don't belong to the Navy." And I said, "No, you don't. All you've got to do is give me the train ticket and let me go home." That's how the hell I got out finally. That was in '47. Okay. So that's my--pretty much my whole career.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you go over to Hawaii? When were you stationed at Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: The first--well, this ship came to the States. The homeport of the Antares was San Pedro, California, but they seldom ever got back to the States. But while I was in receiving out at San Diego and recommissioned the old Ward destroyer, the ship was on its route back to the States. And it came back, and I went aboard that thing in early in '40. Gee, you know, I don't remember. I'd have to get my old--I've got my old record. They gave it to me when I was discharged, and later on the Navy had retained our flight status records from all of the training and that and had them stored down in Texas. And this organization of Silver Eagles, which I belong to, they let us know that the Navy was going to give out all these records if you just sent a note saying you wanted them. And I have all this from all of those years. Now where was I? Was going to--you said--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you get to Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Yeah. I would have gone aboard the thing in the spring of 1940. And as I said, the ship went around to the islands. You know, they were in the process of developing the forward islands in anticipation of, you know, potential engagement with Japan. That was on the burner already way back then. The ship would go from Pearl Harbor, which we really considered our homeport, because we so seldom came back to the States. We would take on a load of cargo, men, equipment or whatever, and go out to Johnson Island, Palmyra Island, Midway, Wake, Phoenix Islands, just all over. And pretty lengthy cruises. So I was on the--I stayed on the Antares for--yeah, a couple years. Yeah, I left in the spring of '42, so I was about two years aboard that thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And it's always described as a repair ship, but it was more than a repair ship actually.

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: No, no, no. It was a supply.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Supply ship?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: A supply called dry stores. It's an AKS. The "AK" is dry stores and supply. And at that time the make-up is you had your formal fighting ships were the destroyer groups, the cruisers, the battleship groups and all that, and the carrier groups. The supply, repair, oilers, and all that were called the base force. So we were a member of the base force. And at that time the secondary ships were going to be protected in the task force or task group by the armed ships and the fighting ships, so there was no guns on there. The oilers didn't have guns. None of the repair ships had guns, nothing. We had no armament to defend. We just, you know--supposedly somebody else is going to protect us. And as a result, that was a very small crew, like 135 officers and men, of which almost 30 of them were officers, so there was only just a little over 100 guys on there running that ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your job on board ship?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: I went in aboard as a fireman. When you enlisted in the Navy, they kind of gave you a choice of if you wanted to pursue the engineering effort or if you wanted to--well, what we called them "deck apes," which were the sailors, the topside sailors who handled the ship and the--oh, I don't know what the hell primarily their duties were. They were just always handling lines and tying the ship up and untying, getting it under way and that sort of thing, and running the boats and stuff. Well, they did the navigation too. We in the "black gang," or the firemen and the engineers down below, of course, fired the boilers. This old ship was also a World War I ship, which had been converted from a coal burner to oil, so we didn't have to shovel oil. But it was a natural draft ship. They hadn't incorporated pressurized firerooms, and it was a hot sun of a gun down there with them boilers. And I had chosen to pursue the engineering. They give us an aptitude test in recruit training, and mine said yeah, you tend toward the engineering. And they--I was given the option, but they recommended give it consideration. So I said yeah, I would. I liked machinery and that and equipment. So I spent almost the first year in the fireroom. And then you graduated into the engine room and learned the engineering functions of the ship's propulsion equipment, generators, and all that. And come off where at that time frame when I came out of the Navy, I could have gone and got a stationary engineer's license just from that experience because I was rather well qualified. So that was the first and the only ship that I was formally ship's company. I had--now, later on in the military I had ridden different ships to get to different stations, but I was never attached to any other, so that was my only one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was it like being stationed in Hawaii back then?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Oh, jeez, it was beautiful. It was absolutely beautiful. You know, there was little or no blacktop, and, god, there were I think the Ala Moana--the Royal Hawaiian and the Ala Moana were the only two hotels. And the tourists, they couldn't afford it I would have to guess, so the tourism wasn't that great. But of course, it was just overwhelmed with sailors because of the Pearl Harbor facility. But it still was an enjoyable place.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things did you do for entertainment?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Me mostly flying. It took all my moneys, you know. And this is another thing. Most of the guys would head for shore and find themselves the prostitutes and the bar and that scene, and none of that. I didn't want that. I was so determined with this flying, and that's pretty expensive. You've got to remember, enlisted at that time frame at 21 bucks a month doesn't go very far. 75 cents a day. You were given your clothing, but you had to buy, you know, your health and comfort stuff, your shaving cream and things like that. And if you smoked or you ate a candy bar or something, why, that came out--nobody gave you those freebies. You just had to pay for everything. Although there was an advantage. Cigarettes, like, which were called sea stores, were tax-free. And they used to put them in little round cans, 50 cigarettes in a can. And of course they were sealed. And you would take the little key and unwind that to keep them fresh. I didn't smoke, so I don't know, but I don't think that they spent more than 50 cents for one of those cans or something, maybe less than that even. 35 cents for a can of cigarettes. So in that respect it wasn't that horrible bad, but you got--after the four months, you went to--you got an automatic raise to 36 dollars a month as a seaman second, and that's where I split off and became a fireman. And from there on you had to take exams to promote. And there was a time element in rate. You couldn't just escalate and go like hell; you had to wait until your turn came around. Then you could take the exam. And man, I'd hit the books and go at it, and I never flunked any of the exams. So when I came off of the Antares in the two years' time frame, I had gone from--I went aboard as seaman second. And the ratings changed to fireman, and a fireman third was the equivalent of a seaman second. So then I went fireman third, fireman second, fireman first class. And machinist mate second class was the low grade petty officer. And came off of there as a second-class petty officer. When I went to the Navy training, that's what I was flying as, a second-class petty officer. But I had time in there. That was almost a year's training, very intensive thing and hell of a lot of effort. And I had gotten married, you know, taken on that responsibility. And jeez, boy, I had my bag full. But I kept at it. When I came out of there a month before I graduated, I was eligible to take the exam for first-class petty officer. Now obviously I wasn't sure I was going to finish the pilot training, and that I'd get kicked out or washed out, so I took the exam for shipboard rating. And also because if I went back to the fleet, then I would go back with one leg up, you know, with first-class petty officer. So I took that exam and became first class. And so my actual diploma or graduation papers for the flight school read as a first-class naval aviation pilot. Now that's the distinction between the commission and the enlisted. The commissioned were naval aviators. The enlisted were naval aviation pilots, NAPs. The old CAS system was in place at that time. They pretty much observed that. There were no blacks. The only blacks were the officers' mess stewards and that sort of thing. Filipinos and blacks did that, but there were no blacks in the regular Navy at that time. At least we didn't have any on the ship that I knew of.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the feeling--go ahead.

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: No. That was a good old ship. That was an ideal duty in that had an opportunity to learn, and we went out into a lot of these forward areas before, you know, there was anything established there. So jeez, when we went to Johnson Island, Johnson Island later on became one of the key air landing strips. And all it was is, you know, a volcanic peak. And when we got there, this one little chunk is sticking out of the ocean. Everybody said, "What the hell they going to do here? An airplane, he can't land by dropping down on that sucker." But they widdled off the top and pushed it both ways and elongated and made an airstrip there. And this same was literally true of Midway Islands. They were just little atolls and--but they got a strip on there. So I really, I really enjoyed the duty on that thing. I made good friendships--well, as witnessed by the fact that, hell, 60-some years later still in contact with these guys. Really enjoyed it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the feeling like on Hawaii? Was there any feeling at all that they were potential targets?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: No, hell no. Nobody would have realized--no. The ocean itself was a barrier. And I don't know that--you know, that's a pretty big ocean, that Pacific area. It's a hell of a long way from there to here, and nobody anticipated--what they did, they sailed that northern route. And you know, I despise the Japanese like everybody else did, and, god, what they did was despicable. At the same time from their standpoint, what they did was very cunning and very sly, and you have to give them credit. I guess, you know, everybody would like to rely on rules of war. War is hell. It's--if you're going to make rules and you can only shoot them until 6 o'clock and then it's dark; you can't shoot them afterwards or something, this kind of thing, the Japs apparently didn't agree that there was any Geneva Convention rules. And what the hell they did was say, Hey, Sunday morning them suckers will all be going to church. Let's just get over there and come on them on a Sunday morning, and they won't be expecting. And that's what the hell happened. They wiped us out, just--yeah, oh, that was a--man, I tell you, that was a low point. I really felt bad as we all did. At the same time we wanted revenge, but we felt pretty badly about having been caught napping like that and just terrible, terrible. And you know, when you're only about 19 years old and you're living a kind of a laid back life-style like that and then all of a sudden, you know, in just a matter of less than an hour almost, this whole chaotic thing happened and the whole damn world turned upside down, and the loss of all your buddies and that. But it sure matured you in a hell of a hurry; I'll say that. You got a little maturity out of that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So the Antares was out of the harbor for a few days before December 7th?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Oh, we were almost two months at sea. We had gone out in October. The Phoenix Islands were British possession. They are--I don't have a globe or anything, but they are out in the South Pacific below the equator, and the British had agreed to allow us, the Americans, to come in and build a runway. The only thing that was operating there was a Pan American seaplane tender station. It was the stopping route for refueling for Pan Am China Clipper. We took a big load of heavy equipment on some barges that we would tow. We would not only load the ship up, but we would tow the barges behind and took the men and equipment to begin constructing runways up there. We left in October and didn't come back until December the 7th. We arrived that morning. And as I said, because they had the submarine net across the mouth of the harbor to prevent, you know, somebody sneaking in, they wouldn't open that until daylight. So having arrived there early in the morning, it was still darkness, the ship just circled it right in the mouth of the harbor. And in fact, when the little submarine attacked us--and this occurred before Pearl Harbor was bombed--in fact, I had the upcoming 8 to 12 watch. Used to stand watches, as they called them, either four on and four off or eight on and eight off. And I had to come up early to eat breakfast to go down and relieve the guys who were down there for them to come up for breakfast and complete their watch. And so I was up like 6 o'clock that morning to--and we were up topside waiting for them to pipe down chow to let you know you can come in and eat. In fact, my one buddy--and he also became a pilot--Harry Ryan. But Mick Ryan and I were standing there on the deck, and we were both looking at this damn submarine coming toward us, and like the guy's going to ram us, and what the hell are they doing? And it didn't look big enough to be a real submarine. And we were wondering what the hell is going on. And the next thing we knew, the Ward, she was the picket destroyer out there. Our ship had called them for assistance, and they came around our bow and kablam, kablam, they shot that sucker right in the conning tower. And that was the first shot fired in World War II, and I sat there watching that thing and didn't know what was going on but had the ringside seat. Now that was at 6:30, and we had decided to chop loose the thing because we couldn't maneuver the ship very well with that tow. We had a tow, a barge. And then about that time, you know, at 7:55, of course, the main attack started. And we chopped that cable, cast that thing adrift so the ship could maneuver. And they made strafing runs and attempted bombing runs, but we being a secondary target, they didn't make the concerted effort they did for the big ships. So we survived everything, and nobody got hit, shot, or hurt.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were outside the harbor when the attack was taking place?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Yeah, and stayed right out there, yeah, yeah. Just kept just making a circle like a lazy eight out there at the mouth of the harbor. So we didn't, at that time frame, didn't see--except for we could see the clouds of the smoke billowing up and the big explosions taking place. In fact, the--probably the largest explosion, even bigger than the Arizona, there was a destroyer in the floating dry dock. I'm trying to remember. Let's see, the Cassin and the Downes were in with the Pennsylvania in the normal dry dock. Oh, I can't think of the--anyway, there was a destroyer in there. And when they hit that sucker, the magazines blew. Boy, we saw the flames from that. They must have went 5, 800 feet in the air. So we knew things were pretty bad or suspecting that things were pretty bad.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Approximately how far out were you from the harbor do you think?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Probably no more than 5 miles at the worst, yeah--no, not even that maybe, a couple miles out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And there was no radio communication that you could hear anywhere--

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Well, because--no. My station when you--when you--in an emergency situation they sound general quarters. Klaxon goes off, you know, and sirens go off, and you go to your appointed station, which mine happened to be the engine room. And that's well below the waterline, and there's no windows down there to look out. And the concussion of the explosions, it's like, you know, the bomb is coming through the--or the torpedo is coming through the side of the hull. You don't know what the hell is happening. And they tell you to constantly inspect the ship's plates to see if the rivets have popped and it's leaking or what the hell's going on. But you're down there in an environment with--you know, if you were up topside and you would be breathing fresh air and seeing what's going on, you would have some degree of security or something or an escape. But you're down there. And I can remember the engineering officer, you know, coming down there strapping on his .45, and these little ladders and catwalks that you go up through to get out of there. He stood at the top and said, "I'm going to shoot the first man that comes up here," because, you know, the guys--I'll tell you, you get into a little bit of a panic situation down there among that machinery and that. You hear these bombs exploding close to you and that impact on the hull. Jesus Christ, man, you know, that just wouldn't seem to be the place you would want to be. We should let you get up topside. So if you're going to sink or something, hell, you've got a Chinaman's chance to get off. But I do remember that. And I got to admit, I was pretty damned concerned.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now these were bombs that they were actually trying to get you--

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Oh, yeah. No, they were trying to bomb us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --or were they concussions from bombs that were falling nearby?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Yeah. Because we were under way and maneuvering the ship, we are a moving target; they didn't do so good with us. All the ships in the harbor, you know, they're actually tied up, just sitting ducks. Couldn't get under way. The only ones that got under way, the battleship Nevada got under way, a couple of the destroyers and that got under way. And even then they bombed the Nevada coming down the channel. So yeah, I guess we were out in the better area in that we could--by maneuvering could avoid being struck.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you finally go into the harbor?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: We--they told us not to come in, to block the channel and to go into Honolulu Harbor. So we went into Honolulu Harbor, and then later that evening we come back into Pearl Harbor. And god, just when you sailed in there, ooh wow, because all the oil on the water and things burning and guys, the bodies. Man, what a mess. That was a very sobering situation. And then that night--because the assumption was that, hell, the Japs are going to take over this place. They're going to bring landing forces. And they had devastated it so that there would be little or no resistance. They should--I don't think they knew how well off they had that. If they had brought some landing forces, I think they could have taken those islands and held them without a hell of a lot of trouble. And that night, that first night, in fact several nights beyond even, they issued us gas masks and--but everybody was a target. You know, you challenged anybody and everybody, and if you didn't get the right answer, you started shooting. And, jeez, boy, we were shooting at each other. There were some untimely deaths. Some--one of the guys on one of the destroyers had a machine gun get away and fired right through the mess deck on one of the--not supply ships, but transports. Killed quite a few guys. Just everybody was so damn trigger happy, it was terrible. Took several days to calm down. Then, of course, nobody had liberty, and, you know, you're confined and what the hell. Everything is dramatically changed. Yeah, probably weren't the most agreeable bunch to get along with.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You mentioned you worked on salvage operations?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Yes, yeah. Because when I was awarded the flight school, I left the ship, and I had to await--my ship was getting ready to leave apparently, and I had to await transportation back to the States on a transport type ship. And that was--I think I was almost a month in the receiving ship, yeah, so--yeah, I was working on the ships. I worked on the West Virginia raising her. I worked on the California, yeah. We were still burying bodies even then. That was a mess, jeez.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And this would be, what, like the spring of '42, right?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: '42, yeah. This would be--if I got back in April--yeah, it was March, March. Even that late yet. Oh, hell, they didn't have the ships raised. They didn't have the Oklahoma turned over. I don't even remember because I left there, I don't know how long it was before that thing--they raised them ships up. They had to kind of build caissons around to make some repairs to be able to pump them out to get them to float to go into the dry dock to make more substantial repairs to get them back to the States. One of the--one of the ships--oh, the Shaw. That's the name, the destroyer Shaw. It was in the floating dry dock, and the bomb that blew the forward magazines and everything cut that ship right in half, sunk the dry dock and the whole works. But here is the back end of this ship of this destroyer almost intact. And they were already building the front end of the ship back in Mare Island Navy Yard. And I remember maneuvering the back end. They had welded some plates over. Looked like somebody took a big hatchet and chopped this sucker off in half. They welded these temporary plates and got it floated, and they brought it alongside our ship. I was still on the Antares. I hadn't gone on the receiving ship yet. And we marveled at the fact--and the reason they brought it to us is because we had a king boom on there which could lift an extremely heavy load, that one big boom up forward. And they had prefabricated a little V-bow to put on this front section of the Shaw, and they were going to sail it back to the States, and they built a little tiny bridge up there, you know, for somebody to steer and see. And we hoisted that bow section out and held it in place while they welded it on to get the Shaw coming back. Yeah, they--that salvage operation in itself had to be a marvelous engineering feat to save what they saved of all of those ships, you know, that were sunk, laying on their sides, and jeez. About the only things they didn't recover--the old Utah was a battleship that was--it was used as a target ship, and it was not a part of the first line Navy. And of course, they didn't salvage the Arizona because that just--that whole hull was just a mess. But rolling that Oklahoma back over--and I've only seen video or films of that because I had already left and wasn't there. But marvelous engineering feat to do that. The West Virginia was sunk. The California was sunk. The Nevada, well, she was beached and sunk. The Oglala. I'm trying to remember all of them, but-- END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were probably down below when the Arizona exploded?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. I didn't see that explosion or--no, I was already down in the--yeah, I had to go down to the engine room and would have been down there, yeah. We didn't--I don't remember when we came back up out of the innards of that ship, but it was somewhere around noon, you know. We could see, you know, up from the water at the mouth of the harbor, we could see all the burning and the fire and the smoke, but could not really see the hulls and the actual superstructure and the devastation. So we went over into Honolulu Harbor. We were there for whatever, four or five hours until evening, and then we came back into the Pearl Harbor, and man, got a real exposure then.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you feel when you saw that?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: What did what?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you personally feel when you saw that?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Well, fright, disgust, hatred, whole combination of feelings, yeah. You know, Frank and I were talking one time. He said, "Oh, I can't imagine you got scared of anything." I said, "Frank, you never spent any time below the water line, and you can't see out. And something is going on, and you're looking to be inundated if the thing, the torpedo comes through or something." I said, "Up topside you had a gun. You could shoot back. We had nothing to shoot back, you know. Very captive feeling there, and a panic feeling, frightened panic feeling." Frank says, "Yeah, but"-- And I says, "I don't know from where you were. It was a different little bit of an environment than from where I was." Yeah. In fact, the damn little two-man sub after they opened the net, one of those got in the harbor, and it was a couple days later when they sunk that sucker.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you know when they sank that that it was Japanese? I mean, obviously--

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --who else would it be?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Then was determined. The one that attacked us that the Ward sunk--now there was still--I think they brought five of these miniatures. One of them, his guidance system didn't work, gyro system or something, and couldn't submerge and do things, couldn't control things, and he beached. And that was the first prisoner of war. They grabbed these two guys from the beached sub. The one that attacked us, which was the very first one and was sunk by the Ward, the one that got into the harbor, I don't know what the hell happened, but I believe there were five of them, and one of them is on display someplace I think down at Fredericksburg, Texas. They have a museum, Halsey Museum or something. One of the famous admirals, you know, was from the Texas area. Or no, maybe it was the guy who was the total overall commander.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Nimitz maybe?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Nimitz. It might be a Nimitz Museum. One of them is down on display down in that area.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the feeling toward the Japanese people on Hawaii after the attack?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Well, I guess equal hatred. They--there was a large contingent. In fact, they used to get the haircut--you weren't supposed to get a normal haircut. You're supposed to--the ship's barber is supposed to cut your hair in a normal military style. But you go ashore, and there was nothing nicer than to get one of them little Jap gals to give you a haircut and climb around. Japanese are pretty nice-looking females, very attractive. I got--I spent time in Japan, and I spent time in China, all the whole China coast, Hong Kong, Shanghai, (Chengdu). I spent time in Sasebo and Yokosuka and Yokahama in Japan. And those are two different distinct style of people. The Chinese are much larger-type people, and they have more protruding foreheads, and the features are quite different than the Japanese, who are smaller people and sloped heads and whatever. But their females are darn pretty women. But yeah, everybody just despised them people for what they did. And, you know, you assume that these guys are part of them even though they were over there before it all came off. Now the Antares, we would supply the inner islands, what they'd call. So while we spent the majority of our time at the Pearl Harbor, we also would go to the Hilo, Hawaii; Kahului, Maui, and offload supplies in there. Now those islands were totally or almost virtually unoccupied by military, just very small contingents, and boy that was really God's country. They didn't have the facilities like Honolulu and that, you know. The communities were--Hilo was much smaller community, but pretty and beautiful and untouched almost. Really nice.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think of Pearl Harbor, does any one thing come to mind as your most vivid experience?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Yeah, I suppose that engineering officer with that gun saying he would shoot the first one of you that come up this ladder. God, because, you know, you're down there, you don't--you know something major is going on from these concussions and all of this. You can't see out, but you don't know what the hell is going on, and you're all talking with each other and grouping and huddling around. And then this guy is standing there and telling you, you know, "You come up this ladder, I'm going to shoot the first guy." Because I think he thought the same thing: we were going to panic and make a break for topside. Yeah, that and that first night. I was given a watch out on the dock, and they said to challenge and, you know, don't hesitate if you don't get the password. And where we used to tie up across from 1010 docks, there were some warehouse segments and that. And Jesus, I remember firing off a few rounds at I don't know whether it was a cat or what the hell it was. But jeez, I wasn't going to wait for somebody if they didn't give me some recognition signal in a hell of a hurry. Shoot, and I shot. And then it would draw fire from somebody else, and pretty soon you're shooting at each other, stupid as could be, yeah. Took a few days to kind of calm down. Then you wondered because, you know, they add to the situation by issuing these gas masks. And when they finally allowed you to go ashore, it was only for a couple hours, and you carried this gas mask along. And, you know, and it's a sharp departure from the peacetime into this whole chaotic situation. You don't make that instantaneous adjustment, you know. It takes a little while to adjust to something like that. Where if you're going into a known war environment, you know what the hell to expect. But jeez, this thing here was--and given the Sunday morning, on a beautiful Sunday morning and church time. You know, just--hooh. You never expected that to happen. And there were--had I got to fly--you ever see the movie "Tora! Tora! Tora!"?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: In the scenes as they open the bombing, the actual bombing scenes, they show a little yellow airplane with a female instructor and a student, and she's caught in between all these Japanese coming in. I would have been in--could have very well been in that airplane had I gotten ashore as I was hoping because I had time scheduled. I would have been out there flying. And that--I knew that young gal, that instructor very well. And in fact, my main instructor was a little Japanese, and he and I built quite a good friendship. Of course, I never went back to the field after the--you know, because they shut the field completely down. But I, you know, respected him as a hell of a good pilot, and he was very insistent on my learning to fly correctly. We flew in this tandem airplane, and he says, "You are just over controlling." He says, "And I'm going to teach you somehow or other." And he says, "What I'm going to do"--he sat in the front seat, and the student sits in the back seat of this tandem situation, but the student's rudder pedals are right up next to the instructor. He said, "Now you take your feet off the pedals, and I'm going to put my hands on the pedals. And you put your feet on my hands." And he said, "If I holler 'ouch,' you're just over controlling. You're hurting my hands." This is how he insisted I flew, and I really had a great deal of respect for him as--of course, that turned to hatred for whatever the hell. He's part of the Jap Empire, so if I could have got him, I would have squashed him. But he did teach me how to fly pretty well.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any particularly vivid memories come to mind from the after Pearl Harbor service time?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: We went--the other one, yeah, was arriving at Okinawa. I didn't get there at the war's end. It was right after, a couple months after. And the devastation, just again, looking at, you know, how much destruction war can wreak. I thought that was pretty bad. But then we flew out of Okinawa and we went up into Japan as occupational, and then flying around there and taking a look at the destruction, the bombings and particularly Hiroshima and Nagasaki, flew over those. And that's a very sobering thing to see. What was these huge communities just a skeletal mess. And you say, one bomb did this? And you know, we've made eons of progress in the few short years since that time. So the next time around, if it really becomes a world conflagration, I don't know what the hell to expect. I won't be here probably, but boy I hope you guys can handle it because it's going to be terrible. You know, you've got somebody like North Korea, you know, that they have missile capabilities and you don't know just what the hell those people are going to do. They are not rational. And if this guy Saddam Hussein gets something, he's going to point those anyplace and pull the trigger, and I don't know, I don't know. I don't know that there will ever be a settlement in that Mideastern region. I have two great-grandsons growing up. And I--in fact, I was just playing Sunday on the floor here with the six-month-older. He and I were having a pretty good time. And I'm just thinking--I had to send the older one a birthday card and some money for his college. And I'm thinking, I wonder what kind of a world they're going to grow up in, I really wonder. I have great faith in the United States. I think old Bush is doing a tremendous job given what he inherited and having this whole thing thrust upon him, just doing an amazing job.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing in the news when they dropped the bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Mmm...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you comprehend what that was all about?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: You know, I'd have to try to remember where was I. Can't say I can remember exactly.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you--

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: I probably would have been in--oh, I think I would have been in operational training down in Florida or Puerto Rico. Yeah, I guess that's what--yeah, okay. Well, yes. Now I do as you are questioning. Because, yeah, we saw that as the flag that said this is the end. Them guys can't handle this anymore and that's going to shut it down, which it did, of course. Now--and I'll give you an example though. When we got into the Yokohama area--well, even at Sasebo, we occupied the Japanese facilities. I was in a C-plane squadron at that time, patrol bombing and air/sea rescue and so forth. But when we occupied their areas, the hangars accompanying the seaplane ramp area and storage area and that, these hangars were stacked full of small speedboats, plywood boat, you know. I don't know whether it's plywood, but real fragile type things. These were kamikazes, just the same as they had with the airplanes at the very end of the war there. They were diving them into the ships and committing the kamikaze act. And some of the men that we had in the workgroups helping attend our airplanes and that as we occupied Japan, these young guys were to pilot those boats out. This was going to be their last-ditch effort to go out and sacrifice themselves. And the front end of these suckers was like a big hunk of TNT. And them boats were stacked up. They were determined not to give in until--obviously they couldn't have been expecting anything like the atom bomb. And when that did happen, that really had to shake them loose because they're very tenacious and--or they were. You know, you know, right now you see a turnaround where they are our ally. We've got to heavily depend on them suckers as a buffer between China and Korea and that. Isn't that crazy how history--sometimes you can't figure it out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where did you celebrate VJ Day; do you know? Do you remember that?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Yeah. I would have been in my operational training because already all the talk and discussion was--yeah, yeah. In fact, they had a meeting at the hangar to advise people, you know, who were speculating and--and of course, a great share of the military was reserve people who had been called in, just as our current situation right now with the military. The actual enlistees and the hardcore was a very small quantity of people. The reservists and the National Guards who had been activated and all of these people. Well, this was true too of World War II. And of course, those guys saw this as an opportunity for them to go home immediately. In fact, they were almost the day after ready to pack their bag and say goodbye. And that was a sort of a chaotic situation, you know, to make the transition back downward, and that let everything fall apart. I do remember, yeah, the day after that they had a meeting in the hangar and were suggesting what they thought might happen in terms of time frame, who goes first and whatever. And that's when I learned also regular Navies don't count on it. You don't get a ticket. You stick around, yeah. Yeah, and it never occurred to me, never occurred to me that my enlistment had expired, and they really didn't have a string on me until this old guy clued me in, yeah. Never occurred to me. So I went two years beyond thinking, well, there's no way. I'm locked in. I can't get out, yeah. I wasn't--you know, up to that point I wasn't that determined to get out, but I had been thinking about it. The reason being there's a guy, a native Clevelander, a guy by the name of Cook Cleland. You probably haven't heard of him. Cleveland was the home of the National Air Races until a very catastrophic accident occurred in which a very responsibly named pilot dove into a house, killed a wife and her baby. And that put the end of the races. But this guy, he was reserve. He and I were in the squadron together, and he got out. And we were communicating. And he says, "Come on home, Beck." He says, "We're going to make all kinds of money in these air races." He says, "I'm getting these surplus Navy fighters. We'll beat the hell out of them in the air races, and we'll take all this money and go home." And boy, that was pretty encouraging. I wanted to get out pretty badly to do that. In fact, I eventually as I did get out--and what cemented my determination was this young--not young, but this same officer who had previously assigned me. He's locked in a nice cushy job there, and he's on shore duty for I don't know how many years because he's reassigning me two years later almost to go back out there. Yeah, that's when I--the determination. But I--yeah, then I did come home, and I did go into the air races, and I didn't win all that much money.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How many years did you race in the air races?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Three years. '47, '48, and '49. I won second place in '47 and in a Thompson, which was the premier event. The other two years didn't fair out so well. Engine troubles. In fact, the last year the engine blew up on me and fortunately made a good landing back at the airport without busting up, yeah. Then--I build airplanes, my own homemade airplanes. I'll show them to you. There's one over there. Very ambitious project. I thought, you know, I had a family of four. My daughters, we'll all build a family airplane. I started building. Took ten years. The kids grew up and left home and didn't get to ride in the airplane. And it was a marginal performer. I found out I wasn't the designer I thought. Oh, I flew it. I proved that one guy could build it and fly it. And I turned around and I built a small high-performance, and I--just two years ago I had a heart attack, and that's when I quit flying. Yeah, I've been flying all these year. Sixty--59 or 60 years of continuous flying. Yeah, I'm pretty proud of my airplane. Last one was a salable item, and a guy in New Hampshire bought it for 25 thou from me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That sounds good.

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: Well, actually--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How much did you put into it?

sp.speaker: Richard M. Becker
sp.p: You know, if you discount your time spent and say, well, I didn't spend all that much time, which you're inclined to do, but in actuality you spend a hell a lot of a time, probably at the 25 grand, I made a dollar an hour off the airplane.
